title: XIV. The Peasants Stand Firm
paragraphs: That was how Fetyukovitch ended his speech, and the audience's enthusiasm broke out like an unstoppable storm. There was no question of holding it back: the women wept, many of the men wept too, even two eminent figures shed tears. The presiding judge gave way, and even put off ringing his bell. To suppress such enthusiasm would have been to suppress something sacred, as the ladies cried afterward. The speaker himself was genuinely moved.

And it was at this very moment that Ippolit Kirillovitch rose to raise certain objections. People looked at him with something like hatred. “What? What does this mean? He actually dares to object,” the ladies muttered. But if every woman in the room, including his own wife, had protested, nothing could have stopped him at that moment. He was pale, shaking with emotion; his first sentences were barely intelligible — he gasped for breath, could hardly get the words out clearly, lost his train of thought. But he soon pulled himself together. Of this second speech of his I'll quote only a few sentences.

“... I'm accused of having spun a romance. But what is this defense, if not one romance piled on top of another? All that was missing was the verse. Fyodor Pavlovitch, while waiting for his mistress, tears open the envelope and throws it on the floor — and we're even told what he supposedly said while doing this strange thing. Isn't that a flight of fancy? And what proof do we have that he actually took the money out? Who heard him say it? The feeble-minded Smerdyakov, transformed into a Byronic hero avenging society for his illegitimate birth — isn't that a romance straight out of Byron? And the son who breaks into his father's house and murders him without murdering him isn't even a romance — it's a sphinx posing a riddle it can't solve itself. If he murdered him, he murdered him — what on earth is the meaning of murdering him without having murdered him? Who can make any sense of that?”

“Then we're told that our tribune is a tribune of true and sound ideas, and from that tribune of ‘sound ideas’ comes a solemn declaration that calling the murder of a father ‘parricide’ is nothing but a prejudice! But if parricide is a prejudice, and every child is entitled to ask his father why he should love him, what becomes of us? What becomes of the foundations of society? What becomes of the family? Parricide, it seems, is nothing but a bogeyman invented to frighten Moscow merchants' wives. The most precious, most sacred guarantees for the destiny and future of Russian justice are being presented to us in a twisted, frivolous form, for one purpose only — to justify what cannot be justified. ‘Oh, crush him with mercy,’ cries the counsel for the defense — but that's exactly what the criminal wants, and tomorrow we'll see just how crushed he is. And isn't the counsel for the defense being too modest, asking only for an acquittal? Why not endow a charity in the parricide's honor, to commemorate his feat for future generations? Religion and the Gospel are being corrected for us — all mysticism, we're told, and ours is the only true Christianity, one that's been run through the sieve of reason and common sense. And so they set before us a false imitation of Christ! ‘Whatever measure you use will be measured back to you,’ cried the counsel for the defense, drawing the instant conclusion that Christ is teaching us to measure others exactly as they measure us — and this, from the tribune of truth and sound sense! We only dip into the Gospel on the eve of making a speech, so as to dazzle the audience with our familiarity with what is, after all, a rather remarkable text, one that can be put to good effect — anything to serve the purpose! But what Christ actually commands is something entirely different: He warns us against exactly this, because that's how the wicked world behaves, and instead tells us to forgive, to turn the other cheek, and not to measure our persecutors by their own measure. That is what our God has taught us — not that forbidding children to murder their fathers is some prejudice. And we will not, from the tribune of truth and sound sense, go about correcting the Gospel of our Lord, whom the counsel for the defense condescends to call merely ‘the crucified lover of mankind,’ in defiance of all Orthodox Russia, which cries out to Him, ‘For Thou art our God!’”

At this point the presiding judge stepped in and reined in the overzealous speaker, urging him not to exaggerate, not to overstep the bounds, and so on, as presiding judges always do in such situations. The audience, too, grew restless; there were even cries of indignation. Fetyukovitch didn't even bother to respond directly; he simply mounted the tribune, laid a hand on his heart, and, in a wounded voice, spoke a few words full of dignity. He touched again, lightly and ironically, on ‘romancing’ and ‘psychology,’ and at the right moment quoted, ‘Jupiter, you are angry, therefore you are wrong,’ which drew a burst of approving laughter from the audience, since Ippolit Kirillovitch bore no resemblance whatsoever to Jupiter. Then, on the subject of being accused of teaching the younger generation to murder their fathers, Fetyukovitch remarked, with great dignity, that he wouldn't even respond to that. As for the prosecutor's charge that he'd voiced unorthodox opinions, Fetyukovitch hinted that this was a personal insinuation, and that he'd expected, in this court, to be safe from accusations ‘damaging to my reputation as a citizen and a loyal subject.’ But the presiding judge cut him off here too, and Fetyukovitch closed his speech with a bow, amid a murmur of approval throughout the court. And in the opinion of our ladies, Ippolit Kirillovitch had been ‘crushed for good.’

Then the prisoner was given leave to speak. Mitya stood up, but said very little. He was terribly worn out, in body and mind alike. The look of strength and independence he'd worn that morning had almost entirely vanished. He seemed to have lived through something that day that had taught him, for the rest of his life, something important he'd never understood before. His voice was weak; he no longer shouted as he once had. There was a new note in his words — humility, defeat, submission.

“What am I to say, gentlemen of the jury? My hour of judgment has come — I feel the hand of God upon me! This is the end for an erring man! But before God, I say it again: I am innocent of my father's blood! For the last time, I say it: it wasn't I who killed him! I went astray, but I loved what is good. Every moment I strove to reform myself, and yet I lived like a wild animal. I thank the prosecutor — he told me a great deal about myself that I didn't know. But it isn't true that I killed my father — the prosecutor is mistaken there. I thank my counsel too. I wept, listening to him. But it isn't true that I killed my father, and he needn't have assumed it. And don't believe the doctors — I'm perfectly sane, only my heart is heavy. If you spare me, if you let me go, I'll pray for you. I'll become a better man. I give you my word before God that I will! And if you condemn me, I'll break my sword over my own head and kiss the pieces. But spare me — don't rob me of my God! I know myself — I'll rebel! My heart is heavy, gentlemen.... spare me!”

He nearly collapsed back into his seat; his voice broke; he could barely get out that last phrase. Then the judges moved on to putting their questions, and asked both sides to formulate their final positions.

But I won't go into the details. At last the jury rose to retire and confer. The presiding judge was exhausted, and so his closing charge to the jury was fairly weak. “Be impartial. Don't let yourselves be swayed by the eloquence of the defense — but weigh the arguments carefully all the same. Remember the heavy responsibility resting on you,” and so on, and so forth.

The jury withdrew, and the court adjourned. People got up, moved around, traded their pent-up impressions, refreshed themselves at the buffet. It was very late, nearly one in the morning, but nobody left — the tension was too great for anyone to think of rest. Everyone waited with a sinking heart — though perhaps that's putting it too strongly, since the ladies were merely in a state of hysterical impatience, their hearts untroubled. An acquittal, they were sure, was inevitable. They were all bracing themselves for a dramatic burst of general rejoicing. I have to admit there were plenty of men, too, who were convinced an acquittal was a certainty. Some were pleased, some frowned, and some were simply gloomy, not wanting to see him acquitted at all. Fetyukovitch himself was confident of success. He was surrounded by people congratulating him, fawning over him.

“There are,” he said to one group, as I was told afterward, “invisible threads that bind the counsel for the defense to the jury. You can feel them forming while you speak. I felt them. They're real. Our case is won. Set your minds at rest.”
“What will our peasants say now?” said one stout, sour-faced, pockmarked gentleman, a landowner from the neighborhood, walking up to a knot of men deep in conversation.
“But they're not all peasants. There are four government clerks among them.”
“Yes, there are clerks,” said a member of the district council, joining the group.
“And did you know that Nazaryev, the merchant with the medal, is on the jury?”
“What of it?”
“He's a man with a head on his shoulders.”
“But he never says a word.”

“He's not much of a talker, but so much the better for it. He doesn't need any lessons from the Petersburg man — he could teach all of Petersburg himself. He's the father of twelve children. Think of that!”
“Surely you don't imagine they won't acquit him?” one of our young officials exclaimed in another group.
“They'll acquit him for certain,” said a confident voice.

“It would be shameful, disgraceful, not to acquit him!” cried the official. “Suppose he really did kill him — there are fathers, and then there are fathers! And besides, he was in such a frenzy.... He may honestly have done nothing but swing that pestle through the air and knock the old man down by accident. But it was a shame they dragged the valet into it — that was simply an absurd theory. If I'd been in Fetyukovitch's place, I'd have just said flatly: ‘He murdered him — but he's not guilty, damn it all!’”
“That's more or less what he did say, only without the ‘damn it all!’”
“No, Mihail Semyonovitch, he all but said that too,” put in a third voice.
“Why, gentlemen, during Lent an actress was acquitted right here in our own town, after cutting the throat of her lover's lawful wife.”
“Oh, but she never finished cutting it.”
“Makes no difference. She started cutting it.”
“What did you make of what he said about children? Splendid, wasn't it?”
“Splendid!”
“And about mysticism too!”
“Oh, forget mysticism, do!” cried someone else. “Think of poor Ippolit and what's coming to him from this day forward. His wife will scratch his eyes out tomorrow over Mitya's acquittal.”
“Is she here?”
“What an idea! If she'd been here she'd have scratched them out right in the courtroom. She's home with a toothache. Heh heh heh!”
“Heh heh heh!”
In a third group:
“I dare say they'll acquit Mitenka after all.”
“I wouldn't be surprised if he turns the ‘Metropolis’ upside down tomorrow. He'll be drinking for ten days straight!”
“Oh, the devil!”
“The devil's bound to have a hand in it somewhere. Where else would he be, if not here?”
“Well, gentlemen, I'll grant it was eloquent. But all the same, it's not the done thing, cracking your father's skull with a pestle! What are we coming to?”
“The chariot! Do you remember that bit about the chariot?”
“Yes — he turned a cart into a chariot!”
“And tomorrow he'll turn the chariot back into a cart, whatever suits him at the time.”
“What crafty fellows there are these days! Is there any justice left in Russia at all?”

But the bell rang. The jury deliberated for exactly one hour — no more, no less. A deep silence fell over the court the moment the audience had taken their seats. I remember how the jurymen filed in. At last! I won't repeat the questions in order — in fact, I've forgotten them. I remember only the answer to the presiding judge's first and most important question: ‘Did the prisoner commit the murder for the sake of robbery, and with premeditation?’ (I don't recall the exact wording.) There was total silence. The jury foreman, the youngest of the clerks, pronounced, in a clear, loud voice, into the deathly stillness of the court:
“Yes, guilty!”

And the same answer followed every question: ‘Yes, guilty!’ — without a single word of mitigation. No one had expected this; nearly everyone had counted on at least a recommendation for mercy. The deathly silence in the court held for a moment — everyone seemed turned to stone, those who'd wanted a conviction no less than those who'd hoped for an acquittal. But that lasted only an instant, and then came a terrible uproar. Many of the men in the audience were pleased; some rubbed their hands together, not even trying to hide their satisfaction. Those who disagreed with the verdict looked crushed, shrugged, whispered to one another, but still seemed unable to take it in. But how can I describe the state the ladies were in? I thought there would be a riot. At first they could hardly believe their ears. Then, all at once, the whole courtroom rang with cries: ‘What does this mean? What next?’ They leapt to their feet. They seemed to imagine the verdict might still be reconsidered, reversed on the spot. At that instant Mitya suddenly stood up and cried out, in a heartbreaking voice, stretching his hands out before him:
“I swear by God and the dreadful Day of Judgment, I am not guilty of my father's blood! Katya, I forgive you! Brothers, friends — have pity on the other woman!”

He couldn't go on; he broke into a terrible sobbing wail that carried through the whole courtroom, in a strange, unnatural voice, unlike his own. From the farthest corner of the back gallery came a piercing shriek — it was Grushenka. She'd managed to talk her way back into the courtroom before the lawyers' closing speeches began. Mitya was led away. The sentencing was put off until the next day. The whole courtroom dissolved into an uproar, but I didn't stay to hear it. I remember only a few remarks I caught on the steps as I went out.
“He'll get twenty years in the mines!”
“Not a day less.”
“Well — our peasants held firm.”
“And finished off our Mitya.”
